title: The ULTIMATE Quads/Legs Exercises Tier-List (Platz-tier to Chicken-tier)
summary: NH ranks quad and knee-flexion exercises from Platz tier (S) down to chicken tier (D). Top picks are heel-elevated squats, Smith machine squats with feet forward, machine belt squats, pendulum leg press, Bulgarian split squats, Platz squats, pendulum hack squats, deficit sumo squats, SSB pause squats and leg extensions, while hybrids, unstable and cardio-based movements are panned. He closes with advice to pick one main squat style plus one variation and to manage lower-back fatigue so legs can be trained often.
claims: Knee flexions and hip hinges should be separated: the best quad exercise can never be the best hamstring exercise
Isolation movements are valuable for legs because they target specific quad areas without fatiguing the whole body
Hybrid movements that try to be both a posterior chain and a quad exercise fail at both
High-bar squats are excellent (A tier), time-tested and how he built his legs, but for many people ankle mobility limits knee travel and they hip-hinge too much
Elevating the heels with squat shoes or small plates fixes high-bar squats, keeping the torso vertical and knees travelling forward: Platz tier
Expect to cut the load by about 20-30% on heel-elevated squats because hamstrings, glutes and lower back contribute less; less weight with more quad stimulus is a win
Learn to squat normally with a barbell before heel-elevated squats; they need skill and proprioception
Beginners should not learn to squat on the Smith machine: free-bar balance is the key skill and the Smith machine teaches the pattern wrong (D tier used that way)
Smith machine squats with feet forward are Platz tier for intermediates and advanced lifters: the knees can travel far forward for a big quad stretch without falling backward
Bodyweight beginner squats (Hindu, bodyweight, wall sits) are only introductory, C tier, and quickly outgrown
The goblet squat is how he learned to squat; it is good for beginners but becomes impractical around 120-130 lb dumbbells: B tier
Front squats are his favorite squat, A tier, but the front rack position is technically demanding and needs wrist flexibility
The machine belt squat is Platz tier: it destroys the quads without loading the spine and needs zero technical skill
Most people misuse the belt squat machine with a wide stance, toes out and forward lean; use a close stance, vertical torso and initiate by pushing the knees forward
Improvised belt squats standing on two platforms are dangerous at failure and the wide stance makes them more glute and adductor work: B tier
The vertical leg press is chicken tier: awkward position, pelvis rounding that endangers the lower back and knees into the chest
Single-leg leg press is C tier: dedicated machines rarely allow a full stretch and on a normal press you must shift off-center
The classic 45-degree leg press is only B tier because better variants exist, though you can build big legs with it
The seated horizontal leg press recruits more quads and less glute and is A tier, but most machines max out around 200 lb, which he can do for 25 reps
Leg training should use heavy loads; legs are extremely strong and he cites 500-600 lb as the sort of weight you should be pressing
A pendulum-style leg press (e.g. Technogym) fixes the strength curve and feel: Platz tier, but rare and expensive
Banded lying leg extensions are chicken tier: impossible to overload, only for warm-ups or knee rehab
Walking lunges are the worst single-leg option (C tier): limited by cardio and grip, inconsistent reps; static lunges are better (B tier)
Split squats are A tier; avoid bumping the back knee on the floor to cheat the rep
Bulgarian split squats are Platz tier; elevating the back leg removes it from the effort so you get more out of less weight
If Bulgarian split squats are not the exercise you dread most, you are cutting range of motion or skipping the negative
He would rather do 10x10 of paused high-bar squats than 3 sets of 10 Bulgarian split squats, but still keeps them because they work
Do Bulgarian split squats with dumbbells rather than a barbell to avoid leaning into a hip hinge and having to balance a bar
Step-ups are chicken tier for hypertrophy: limited knee flexion and no negative
Explosive squats, jump squats and box jumps are C tier for hypertrophy
Shrimp squats are C tier; pistol squats are B tier with good range but a hard-to-control negative that can strain the knee tendons
Calisthenics athletes claiming pistols build big legs still have small legs; split squats are more effective with less skill and balance
Sissy squats are A tier, not knee destroyers, if done strictly with a slow negative; start band-assisted; best bodyweight quad isolation
The Platz squat (high bar, very close stance, toes forward, heels elevated, vertical torso) is the most quad-dominant squat; expect to halve your back-squat weight: Platz tier
Up-and-down leverage squat machines are pointless, and the lever 'calf/quad' machines can snap your lower back: C tier
Reverse hack squats defeat the purpose by letting the hips travel back into a hinge: B tier
The regular hack squat is A tier, but its strength curve has an unbeatable sticking point where hip and knee align, making true failure hard
The pendulum hack squat is Platz tier: spares the lower back, huge range of motion, can grind and get partner assistance on the positive, easy on the knees
Dumbbell leg extensions are chicken tier: bad strength curve and maximal knee shear at the top
The king squat, a good morning/squat hybrid, is C tier: no load suits both patterns
Jefferson squats are B tier: limited range, staggered stance and possible imbalances
Barbell hack squats are A tier; Silver and Golden Era bodybuilders credited them for big quads and the spine is not loaded
The deficit sumo squat is to knee flexions what the RDL is to hip hinges: Platz tier; initiate with the knees and keep a vertical torso
Sumo deadlifts are chicken tier for legs: mostly a hip hinge with poor range and stimulus-to-fatigue ratio
He doubts EMG data showing trap-bar deadlifts are great for quads; it is still a hinge: C tier
Sumo shiko stomping is C tier for size: bodyweight only and not scalable
Low-bar squats are B tier for bodybuilders, only for those who cannot high-bar; more weight does not mean more quad recruitment
Box squats for novices make no sense; done with a low box, vertical torso and no rocking or resting, they are A tier for quads
The SSB is the best implement for pause squats because the bar cannot shift and form does not degrade: Platz tier
Rowing machines and air bikes are chicken tier for legs; people who did rowing instead of leg day kept chicken legs
The adductor machine is A tier pure isolation for the adductors without taxing the lower back
Leg extensions are Platz tier; you only hurt your knees on them by using idiotic loads, and they are a rare true quad isolation
Bosu or unstable-surface squats are chicken tier; overhead squats are C tier for bodybuilders
Zercher squats are B tier; zombie squats are A tier, less technical but less stable than front squats
Pick one main squat style and one variation, get stronger at them, then fill the volume gap with less fatiguing isolation movements
Lower-back fatigue is often the limiting factor in leg training; manage it so you can train legs hard and often
